claims.text: Population density is the number of people per unit area, people per square kilometre, worked as total population divided by area; population distribution is where people live and where they do not, the pattern of spread, and it is described as a pattern, not by naming scattered places.

claims.text: Each factor must be linked to the way it pushes density: steep relief makes farming and building hard, so density is low on high mountains; flat, fertile lowland supports farms and cities, so density is high; reliable rain and rivers raise density where dry climates lower it.

claims.text: Economic and human factors move density too: jobs, ports and trade routes attract people and raise density, while poor access, weak soils and few jobs thin a population out.

claims.text: Sparse population is caused by physical and economic factors, relief, climate, water, soils, access and jobs; a shortage of services is a consequence of sparse population, not one of its causes.

claims.text: The Ganges delta in Bangladesh is one of the densest rural areas on Earth: the country averages around 1125 people per square kilometre (2022) and the delta districts run higher still, a dense population resting on flat, fertile, well-watered land.

claims.text: The delta supports its density because annual floods renew the soil for rice, the rivers give water and transport, and three harvests a year are possible, which means the same hectare feeds far more people than dryland farming could.

claims.text: The Namib Desert coast of Namibia is sparsely populated: the Erongo and Kunene regions along it hold only a few people per square kilometre, against Windhoek's thousands, because the coast receives under 50 millimetres of rain a year.

claims.text: The Namib's sparse population rests on its physical limits: almost no rain, so neither crops nor herds can live off the land, and the cold ocean and strong winds the coast adds make settled farming harder still, so the people who do live there cluster at the few places with water, Walvis Bay and the mining towns.

claims.text: Sparse populations like the Namib coast keep few services, not because services cause the emptiness but because the few people cannot support schools, clinics and shops within reach, which is a consequence of the low density rather than a cause of it.
